package_info.why_malicious: ExelaStealer is a purpose-built infostealer targeting Windows systems. It is designed to covertly collect a wide range of sensitive information—including credentials, system and user details, clipboard data, screenshots, and Wi-Fi profiles—without user consent. The malware employs code obfuscation, masquerades as legitimate processes, and exfiltrates stolen data to attacker-controlled infrastructure via Discord webhooks, making it a significant threat to user privacy and system security.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code executes Windows system commands to retrieve the OS version and the hardware UUID, then stores this information for later exfiltration to the attacker's infrastructure.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Collecting the hardware UUID and system version is a common tactic for malware to uniquely fingerprint victim machines and facilitate targeted attacks.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not silently collect hardware UUIDs and system version information without explicit user consent or a clear, disclosed purpose.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Enterprise asset management or inventory tools may collect such data, but only with user awareness and typically in managed environments.
key_indicators: Execution of system commands for host fingerprinting

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code invokes PowerShell to extract image data from the clipboard and saves it as a PNG file in a temporary directory named after the host's UUID, without user interaction.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Accessing and saving clipboard image data without user knowledge is a privacy violation and can expose sensitive information such as screenshots or copied images.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal applications do not silently extract and store clipboard images in hidden or system directories without explicit user action.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Screenshot utilities or clipboard managers may save clipboard images, but only with clear user interaction and notification.
key_indicators: Saving clipboard images to hidden, UUID-named temp directories
No user prompt or visible indication

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: C:\Windows\system32\cmd.exe /c "echo ####System Info#### & systeminfo & echo ####System Version#### & ver & echo ####Host Name#### & hostname & echo ####Environment Variable#### & set & echo ####Logical Disk#### & wmic logicaldisk get caption,description,providername & echo ####User Info#### & net user & echo ####Startup Info#### & wmic startup get caption,command & echo ####Firewallinfo#### & netsh firewall show state "
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code executes a series of Windows commands to collect comprehensive system information—including OS details, environment variables, disk information, user accounts, startup programs, and firewall status—and stores the results for later exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Bulk collection of detailed system and user information is a hallmark of infostealer malware, enabling attackers to profile victims and facilitate further exploitation.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not aggregate such a wide range of sensitive system data without user consent or a clear, disclosed purpose.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: System diagnostic or support tools may collect some of this data, but typically with user awareness and for troubleshooting purposes.
key_indicators: Comprehensive system reconnaissance via multiple Windows commands
Aggregation of environment variables, user accounts, and startup info

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
netsh wlan export profile
C:\Windows\system32\cmd.exe /c "netsh wlan show profile"
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code executes Windows commands to export and enumerate all saved WLAN profiles on the system, potentially exposing stored Wi-Fi credentials, and saves the output for later exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Exporting WLAN profiles can reveal Wi-Fi credentials, which are highly sensitive and can be used for lateral movement or further attacks.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal applications do not access or export WLAN profiles without explicit user intent or notification.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Network troubleshooting or migration tools may access WLAN profiles, but only with user initiation and awareness.
key_indicators: Export of WLAN profiles using netsh
No user interaction or visible prompt

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Files are packaged into a Zip archive using the UUID as the filename, then sent using a Discord webhook (https://discord.com/api/webhooks/1139506512302194789/X_VYZdAHscWQ)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After data collection, the code compresses all gathered files into a zip archive named after the host's UUID and exfiltrates the archive to an attacker-controlled Discord channel via a webhook.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Exfiltrating sensitive data to a third-party service such as Discord via webhooks is a clear sign of malicious intent and data theft.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not send user or system data to Discord webhooks, especially without user knowledge or consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Bug reporting or diagnostic tools may upload logs, but never to Discord webhooks and always with user awareness.
key_indicators: Use of Discord webhook for automated data exfiltration
Packaging of sensitive data into zip archives in temp directories
Outbound network connection to Discord API

attack_chain.action: Initial execution of the dropper binary, which unpacks and runs the main ExelaStealer payload and displays a decoy PDF to distract the user.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of the main infostealer logic

attack_chain.action: Collection of system version and hardware UUID for victim fingerprinting.
attack_chain.leads_to: Further system and user data collection

attack_chain.action: Extraction and saving of clipboard image data.
Bulk collection of system, user, disk, environment, and firewall information.
Export and enumeration of WLAN profiles to potentially steal Wi-Fi credentials.
Packaging of all collected data into a zip archive named after the host UUID.
Exfiltration of the zip archive to an attacker-controlled Discord webhook.
attack_chain.leads_to: Completion of attack; attacker receives stolen data

behavioral_signatures: Execution of system reconnaissance commands (systeminfo, wmic, net user, netsh, hostname, set, netsh wlan export profile)
Silent clipboard access and saving of clipboard images to hidden or UUID-named directories
Export and enumeration of WLAN profiles without user interaction
Packaging of user/system data into zip archives in temp directories named after hardware UUIDs
Network communication to Discord webhooks for automated data exfiltration
file_indicators: Temporary directories in %TEMP% named after hardware UUIDs
Zip archives in temp folders with UUID-based names
network_indicators: Outbound HTTPS connections to Discord webhook endpoints
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for processes—especially those masquerading as legitimate Windows executables—that execute system reconnaissance commands (systeminfo, wmic, net user, netsh, hostname, set), access clipboard data, or export WLAN profiles. Flag creation of zip archives in temp directories with UUID-based names. Detect outbound network traffic to Discord webhook URLs, particularly following recent file compression or data aggregation activity. Look for the presence of known file indicators such as 'sirket-ruhsat-pdf.exe', 'Obfuscated.py', and UUID-named zip files in temp folders. Correlate these behaviors to identify infostealer activity.
